# Sex structure

Many stocks are sexually dimorphic: in anglerfish, hake or many flatfish, females grow larger and live
longer than males. A one-sex model fitted to the combined lengths then reads the many small
males as heavy fishing, and status, which is about female spawning, is biased. FLicc's
sex-structured option models females and males as two growth-type-group populations that share
fishing mortality and selectivity, each with its own growth, natural mortality, weight and
maturity, and fits length samples that are combined, sexed or both, as in Stock Synthesis.

The example is a simulated stock (`data(sexsim)`): females reach Linf 60 cm with k 0.15, males
45 cm with k 0.25, M = 0.3 for both. A trawl fishery has unsexed samples; a survey has sexed
samples from 2016.

```{r sex-data}
data(sexsim)
lhpar_sexsim
lapply(lfd_sexsim, function(q) dimnames(q)$unit)
```

## Length data by sex

Sex is carried in the FLR `unit` dimension of each gear's length frequencies, with levels `F`,
`M` and `U` (unsexed; `unique` is read as unsexed). For each gear and year FLicc reads which
sexes have counts and uses the composition in the same way as Stock Synthesis:

| Stock Synthesis gender code | units with counts | compared with |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | `U` | the predicted composition of females and males together |
| 1 | `F` only | the composition within females |
| 2 | `M` only | the composition within males |
| 3 | `F` and `M` | one joint composition over length and sex: the sex ratio at length is information |

Combined and sexed samples can sit in the same gear-year (partly sexed samples), and gears and
years can differ. A long table with a `sex` column (F, M, U; female, male, unsexed; or the SS3
codes 1, 2, 0) is converted as usual:

```{r sex-long, eval = FALSE}
lfd <- FLQuantLen(lfd_long_to_wide(df_long_with_sex), unit = "cm")
```

`lfdess()` rescales females and males of a sample together, so the sex ratio is kept, and
unsexed fish separately.

`plot_lfd()` shows length data with sexes in the style of r4ss: one panel per year and gear,
females above the horizontal line (red), males below (blue), and unsexed samples in their own
column (grey). This view is used automatically when any gear has F or M units (`sex = FALSE`
switches it off). With `type = "prop"` each sexed sample is a proportion over both sexes, so the
sex ratio at length can be read directly:

```{r sex-lfd, fig.height = 6}
plot_lfd(FLQuants(lapply(lfd_sexsim, function(q) q[, ac(2021:2025)])), type = "prop")
```

## Life history by sex

`stocklen_sex()` builds one stock object per sex. The female stock is the reference: SPR is
female spawning potential and F is scaled by the female k. The simplest input is the usual
one-sex `lhpar` (taken as the females) plus the male values that differ; all other male
parameters are copied from the females. `lhpar_sex()` makes the same `FLPar` by sex, to check or
store it:

```{r sex-lhpar}
lh_F <- FLPar(lhpar_sexsim@.Data[, "F", 1], params = dimnames(lhpar_sexsim)$params)
lhpar_sex(lh_F, linf = 45, k = 0.25, L50 = 28)
```

so that `stocklen_sex(lfd, lh_F, male = list(linf = 45, k = 0.25, L50 = 28))` and
`stocklen_sex(lfd, lhpar_sex(lh_F, linf = 45, k = 0.25, L50 = 28))` are the same. An `FLPar`
with a `unit` dimension (as returned by `ss3diags2::ss3_lhpar()`) or `list(F = , M = )` is
accepted as well.

```{r sex-stock}
stk_sex <- stocklen_sex(lfd_sexsim, lhpar_sexsim, m_model = "constant")
plot_growth(stk_sex, sex = "M")
```

## Fitting

Gears named in `settings$surveys` are surveys: their composition is the population seen through
the survey's selectivity, with no fishing mortality and no share of the catch, so
`catch_by_gear` is given for the fishery gears only. `settings$sex_ratio` is the proportion of
females at recruitment (default 0.5).

Four fits show what the sex structure buys. The first ignores sex (female life history, trawl
only); the second models both sexes from the unsexed trawl samples; the third adds the sexed
survey. The fourth starts from a wrong male Linf (52 instead of 45) and estimates it with a
penalty:

```{r sex-fits}
sf2 <- c("dsnormal", "logistic")
set_s <- list(obs_model = "mn", surveys = "Survey")

trawl_U <- FLQuants(Trawl = lfd_sexsim$Trawl[, , "U"])
fit_1sex <- fiticc(trawl_U, stocklen(trawl_U, lh_F, m_model = "constant"), sel_fun = "dsnormal",
                   catch_by_gear = 1, settings = list(obs_model = "mn"))
fit_2sex_U <- fiticc(FLQuants(Trawl = lfd_sexsim$Trawl), stocklen_sex(trawl_U, lhpar_sexsim, m_model = "constant"),
                     sel_fun = "dsnormal", catch_by_gear = 1, settings = list(obs_model = "mn"))
fit_sex <- fiticc(lfd_sexsim, stk_sex, sel_fun = sf2, catch_by_gear = 1, settings = set_s)
fit_sex_est <- fiticc(lfd_sexsim, stocklen_sex(lfd_sexsim, lh_F, male = list(linf = 52, k = 0.25, L50 = 28),
                                              m_model = "constant"),
                      sel_fun = sf2, catch_by_gear = 1, settings = modifyList(set_s, list(linf_m.sd = 0.3)))

runs <- list(one_sex = fit_1sex, two_sex_trawl = fit_2sex_U, two_sex_survey = fit_sex,
             male_Linf_est = fit_sex_est)
tab <- data.frame(year = truth_sexsim$year, true = round(truth_sexsim$spr, 3),
                  sapply(runs, function(f) round(as.numeric(f$report$spr), 3)))
tail(tab, 5)
fits_summary(runs)[, c("run", "conv", "SPR", "lwr", "upr", "Linf_M", "Mk_M")]
```

The one-sex fit underestimates SPR most, because the small males are read as heavy fishing.
Modelling both sexes with their life history reduces the bias even from unsexed samples, and the
sexed survey reduces it further: it informs the selectivity of small fish and the sex ratio at
length, and with it the male growth, so that the estimated male Linf moves from 52 back to about
45. All fits are lowest in the last years, where the equilibrium model lags the rising F
(chapter *Fishing mortality over time*).

**Life-history penalties by sex.** Linf, M/k and CVL are separate parameters for each sex, each
fixed at its input unless a penalty (prior SD on the log scale) is given:

| | females | males |
|---|---|---|
| Linf | `linf.sd` | `linf_m.sd` |
| M/k | `Mk.sd` | `Mk_m.sd` |
| CVL | `CVL.sd` | `CVL_m.sd` (input `CVL_m`, default `CVL`) |

One sex can be fixed while the other is estimated. Sexed samples, especially joint female and
male samples, carry the information; with unsexed data only, the male parameters are weakly
determined and are best kept fixed or under informative penalties. M/k is usually best fixed.

## Diagnostics by sex

`plot_sexratio()` compares the observed proportion of females at length in the joint samples
with the prediction. The prediction follows from the growth and M of each sex and the sex ratio
at recruitment; a rising share of females at large lengths is the usual signature of females
growing larger. Observed proportions above or below the line over a range of lengths point to
male growth, M by sex or the sex ratio; misfit only at small lengths often reflects small fish
that could not be sexed.

```{r sex-ratio, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_sexratio(fit_sex)
```

`plot_len()` shows the fits in the same mirrored layout: observed proportions as bars and the
fit as lines, females above and males below the line, unsexed samples in their own column. A
sample with both sexes is shown as one joint composition over length and sex, as it enters the
likelihood (the areas above and below the line sum to one), and a sample of one sex as a
composition within that sex. `sex = "panels"` gives one panel per gear and sex instead. The
residuals and predictive checks include the sexed samples, with one panel per gear and sex:

```{r sex-len, fig.height = 6}
plot_len(fit_sex, year = 2021:2025)
plot_resid_bubble(fit_sex, type = "osa")
```

## Status and reference points

Spawning potential is female spawning output; yield sums both sexes. `eqstklen()`,
`plot_eqcurves()`, `flicc2FLStockR()` and `flicc_stklen()` return ordinary one-unit FLR objects
in which catch is that of both sexes and SSB the female spawning biomass (with a catch-weighted
mean weight and an effective maturity at length), so all FLR tools work unchanged. Contours,
EPR and the Monte Carlo (`mc_flicc()`, life history of both sexes drawn with the same relative
deviations) use both sexes as well.

```{r sex-eq, fig.height = 5}
eq_sex <- eqstklen(fit_sex, s = 0.75)
attr(eq_sex, "refpts")
plot_eqcurves(eq_sex)
```

## Indicators by sex

`lbi_flicc()` computes the empirical indicators for each sex from its own samples and life
history (`sex = "each"`, the default with sexed data; gears labelled "gear F", "gear M"),
for one sex, or for all fish together (`sex = "total"`, with pooling by catch):

```{r sex-lbi, fig.height = 5}
plot_lbi(lbi_flicc(fit_sex))
```

## Model

For each sex $s$ the growth-type-group recursion of chapter *Model equations* runs with the
sex's own $L_{\infty,s}$, CVL$_s$ and $M_s/k_s$. Fishing mortality at length is shared,
$F(L) = \sum_g F_g S_g(L)$; in the units of each sex's growth it is $F(L)/k_s$, i.e. FLicc's
$F/k$ (female) times $k_F/k_s$. Numbers per recruit in a length class are integrals over the time
spent in it, so the male numbers are put on the female time scale by $k_F/k_M$, and recruits
are split by the sex ratio $\rho$ (proportion female):
$$
N(L) = \rho\, N_F(L) + (1-\rho)\,\frac{k_F}{k_M}\, N_M(L),
\qquad C_g(L) = N(L)\, F_g S_g(L).
$$
A combined composition is compared with $C_g(L)/\sum_L C_g(L)$; a joint sexed composition with
the cells $\rho N_F(L) F_g S_g(L)$ and $(1-\rho)(k_F/k_M) N_M(L) F_g S_g(L)$, normalised over
both sexes; a one-sex composition within that sex. Surveys replace $F_g S_g(L)$ by $S_g(L)$.
SPR is female: $\sum_L N_F(L)\,m_F(L)\,w_F(L)$ fished over unfished. Yield per recruit sums
$\rho$ times the female and $1-\rho$ times the male yield.

## Notes and limits

- Fishing mortality and selectivity are shared by the sexes; differences in availability by
  sex (a selectivity offset) are not modelled yet.
- The sex structure is available for the growth-type-group model (`pop_model = "gtg"`).
- Sexing that depends on length (small fish left unsexed) is handled only in so far as the
  unsexed fish enter as a combined composition; the sexed composition assumes sexing is random
  within a length class.
- `flicc.sa()` runs the sex-structured estimator in MSE when `lhpar` is given by sex.
